entries.q: What is Exe Protocol?
also: what does exe do
explain exe protocol simply
what is the exe execution layer
entries.html:
Exe Protocol is the execution layer for apps, wallets and agents. Exe Protocol prices every payment by your XPR, your Exe Protocol Rate, earned through your verified on-chain signal.

Apps plug in through an SDK (in development), with your XPR designed to carry to every app built on Exe Protocol. Each wallet’s activity, whether a person’s or an agent’s, pays for its execution.

entries.q: What problem is Exe solving?
also: why does exe need to exist
what problem does exe protocol solve
why would anyone need exe
why bother with exe
what is wrong with paying the usual way
what hassle does this remove
entries.html: AI agents are starting to pay at machine speed and scale, creating two problems: settling every payment on-chain adds cost, and an autonomous agent needs firm spending limits. Exe Protocol settles payments in netted batches, sets spending limits up front, and prices each fee by the payer’s signal: smarter, so faster and cheaper.

entries.html:
Exe Protocol is built for smarter, cheaper machine-speed execution across wallets, apps and autonomous agents.

Apps and their agents use Exe Protocol through an SDK (in development): trading apps, Telegram apps, and AI agents and services. Every wallet, user or agent earns its own XPR.

entries.q: What is Exeswap?
also: what does exeswap do
is exeswap a dex
explain the exeswap app
entries.html:
Exeswap is a DEX aggregator, and the first app built on Exe Protocol. Exeswap finds the cheapest swap route for your trade (to be verified before launch), then your XPR reduces the fee by 0–100% depending on your signal strength.

A working prototype you can try today: launch Exeswap.

entries.q: What is XPR?
also: what does xpr stand for
explain the exe protocol rate
what is my xpr rate
entries.html:
XPR, your Exe Protocol Rate, functions as your personalized ‘exchange rate,’ with higher XPR meaning lower fees, from 0–100%. Earned through verified on-chain signal, XPR is determined by your activity.

XPR powers Exeswap and is designed to carry across every app that uses Exe Protocol.

also: can I use exeswap without xpr
is xpr compulsory

entries.html: No. XPR is opt-in. Without it, Exeswap works as a regular aggregator and you pay the normal fee.

entries.q: How does my XPR go up or down?
also: does my xpr change each month
how quickly does xpr update
does xpr remember earlier activity
does my rate move each month
how much does last month count
does my old rate still matter
entries.html: Your XPR follows your verified on-chain activity: steady activity builds your XPR, and a period of less activity, even inactivity, lowers it gently. Your history counts too, so one burst of activity can’t send your XPR soaring, and one quiet period won’t wipe it out.

entries.q: What are Tiers and how do they work?
also: What are tiers?
How do tiers work?
What's the difference between Tier 1, 2 and 3?
Explain the tiers
How many tiers are there?
entries.html: Tier 1 is where everyone starts. Tier 2 adds a budget commitment, earns more from the same XPR, and lets your XPR go up to 1.10. Tier 3 earns more again, so your fees stay low even in a quieter month.

entries.q: Can XPR go above 1.00?
also: what is the maximum xpr
is xpr capped at one
why does xpr go up to 1.10
how high can my rate go
is one the limit
can the rate reach one point one
entries.html:
Yes, at Tiers 2 and 3. XPR runs from 0.00 to 1.00, and up to 1.10 at Tiers 2 and 3. Tier 1 is never above 1.00.

Either way, a user never redeems more than the fees they paid.

entries.q: Why can two wallets with the same XPR pay different fees?
also: does the same xpr always give the same fee
why is my fee different at the same rate
what else affects fee redemption
same rate why a different bill
what changes my cost besides xpr
why do two people on the same rate pay different amounts
entries.html:
Because XPR isn't the only factor. Higher tiers earn more from the same XPR, gas differs from chain to chain, and pool strength sets how much of what XPR earns Exe's pool can pay right now.

Every quote shows the full fee, what XPR redeems and what you pay.

entries.q: What does Tier 1 give me?
also: how does tier one work
what is the starting tier
what do I get at the basic tier
entries.html:
At Tier 1, with Exe's pool at full strength, your fee redemption matches your XPR: XPR 0.60 redeems 60% of each trade's fee.

At Tier 1, XPR runs up to 1.00.

entries.q: How do I reach Tier 2?
also: how do I qualify for tier two
what budget is needed for tier 2
how do I move up from tier one
entries.html:
Set aside a budget in your own wallet, usually about 10% (between 5% and 25%, lower for a long, steady history) of what you trade in a month. The budget stays in your wallet, and Exe Protocol never holds it. A new budget counts once you’ve held it for 30 days.

Tier 2 earns more from the same XPR, and lets your XPR go up to 1.10.

entries.q: How do I reach and keep Tier 3?
also: how do I qualify for tier three
what keeps me in tier 3
when would I drop from tier three
entries.html:
Stay at Tier 2 with an XPR of 0.75 or more for four months in a row. Tier 3 earns more again, so your fees stay low even in a quieter month.

Two months below 0.75 and you move back to Tier 2.

entries.q: Does committing a bigger budget raise my XPR?
also: can I increase xpr by committing more money
does a larger budget improve my rate
can I buy a higher xpr
entries.html: No. A budget above the minimum is headroom for a busier month only. It does not raise XPR: fee redemption is earned through signal, never bought.

entries.q: What happens if I end my Tier 2 or Tier 3 budget commitment?
also: can I stop the tier budget commitment
what happens if I withdraw my tier budget
do I lose my tier when the commitment ends
can I leave tier two
what if I take my budget out
do I drop a tier if I stop committing money
entries.html: You can withdraw your budget at any time, and you drop back to Tier 1. The budget stays in your own wallet; Exe Protocol never holds it.

entries.q: What fees does Exeswap model?
also: what is the normal exeswap fee
does exeswap charge gas as well
what do I pay before xpr

what fees do I pay

entries.html: Each trade costs the network’s gas plus Exe Protocol’s fee: 0.10% of the trade on low-fee chains, 0.25% on Ethereum. XPR redeems a share of that total.

entries.q: What would XPR 0.60 mean on a $1,000 swap?
also: show me a simple xpr fee example
what does 0.60 xpr save in the example
work out the illustrated thousand dollar swap

A $1,000 trade on a low-fee chain costs $1.01: a $1.00 protocol fee plus $0.01 gas. At Tier 1, with Exe’s pool at full strength, XPR 0.60 gives a fee redemption of $0.61, all from the user's own fees. The user pays $0.40.

Simulated.

entries.q: What is the Sponsorship Pool?
also: what is exes pool
what does sp mean
what is the shared sponsorship pool for
what is that shared pot
what does the pool actually do
what is the pool for
entries.html:
Exe's shared pool. Your XPR determines how much of your fee is redeemed from Exe’s pool, after what your own fees cover.

The pool is funded by 70% of Exe Protocol’s revenue. Users’ budgets and wallet balances never enter the pool.

entries.q: How is the Sponsorship Pool funded?
also: where does money for the pool come from
what pays for shared fee redemption
does the pool use user balances
where does the pool get its money
does the pool take my wallet money
how does money get into the shared pot
entries.html:
By 70% of Exe Protocol’s revenue, from Exeswap’s fees and the protocol fees that apps’ users pay. The other 30% goes to operations.

Users’ budgets and wallet balances never enter the pool.

entries.q: Where does my fee redemption come from?
also: why does the example split fee support into two parts
what does from my own fees mean
how is own-fee support different from pool support
what is the difference between own-fee support and shared pool support
entries.html:
First from your own fees: up to 70% of the protocol fee you paid. The rest comes from Exe’s pool.

The part from your own fees never shrinks, whatever the pool’s state. Fee redemption never exceeds the fee you paid.

entries.q: What happens when the pool cannot cover all demand?
also: what happens when pool strength drops
can the pool pay less under load
why would shared fee support decrease
entries.html:
If Exe’s pool runs low, everyone’s share from the pool shrinks equally. The part paid from your own fees depends only on your XPR, never on pool strength.

Under load, the pool steps down gradually. In all nine stress tests (simulated, 24 months each), the pool never ran dry.

entries.q: Does one app pay for another app's users?
also: are app pool balances kept separate
do apps subsidise each other
is there a separate account for each app
entries.html:
No. Each app has its own account in the pool, built from the fees its users pay, so no app subsidises another.

Exe Protocol starts each new app’s account with about 1.9 months of its expected income.

No. Nothing is required from apps for fee redemption.

An app can fund a budget so XPR also discounts its own fee. That money goes to its users under the same rules.

entries.q: Who pays when an AI agent makes a payment?
also: who funds an agent transaction
does the agent or its owner pay
who covers an agent's fees
entries.html:
The payer pays: the fee falls on whoever funds the agent’s budget, the app or its user.

Set the budget and limits up front, and the agent is designed to pay on its own, instantly: no human, no crypto housekeeping.

entries.q: How would Exe work with x402?
also: is exe a replacement for x402
what does exe add to x402
how do x402 and exe fit together
entries.html:
x402 moves the money; Exe Protocol determines what it costs, by signal.

x402 is the pipe, not the rival. Exe Protocol adds what x402 does not have: fees priced by the payer’s signal, budgets and policy set before each payment, a shared pool that funds fee redemption, and settlement netted across all agents. (Working with any rail is a statement of intent until built.)

entries.q: What does net settlement mean?
also: why do you batch payments
how does netting work
why are there fewer settlements than payments
entries.html:
Each payment is approved and recorded instantly, then settled on-chain later in netted batches. Fewer settlements mean lower costs than typical on-chain transactions that settle every payment individually.

In the agent-payments simulation: 22.8× fewer on-chain transactions.

entries.q: Where would an agent's budget be held?
also: is agent budget escrow already built
who holds agent payment funds
how would agent budget custody work
entries.html:
Planned: each agent’s budget sits in an escrow contract the agent controls. A batch settles only payments the agent signed.

The prototype doesn't do this yet, and no real money moves.

entries.q: How fast is Exe?
also: how fast is the prototype fee calculation
what was timed at 0.054 milliseconds
does 18406 a second mean real payments per second
what does the 0.054 ms measurement actually cover
entries.html:
In the prototype, determining a payment’s fee relief takes 0.054 ms: 18,406 a second on one computer, in memory. Netting 100,000 payments between 1,000 agents takes 0.9 ms.

Both measured in the prototype, not on a live network.
